Multi-Agent Conformal Prediction with Personalized Statistical Validity

Martin V. Vejling Affiliation: Department of Electronic Systems Affiliation: Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark Email: mvv@es.aau.dk    Christophe A. N. Biscio Affiliation: Department of Mathematical Sciences Affiliation: Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark Email: christophe@math.aau.dk    Adrien Mazoyer Affiliation: Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse Affiliation: Université de Toulouse, Toulouse, France Email: adrien.mazoyer@math.univ-toulouse.fr    Petar Popovski Affiliation: Department of Electronic Systems Affiliation: Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark Email: petarp@es.aau.dk    Shashi Raj Pandey Affiliation: Department of Electronic Systems Affiliation: Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark Email: srp@es.aau.dk
Abstract

Uncertainty quantification is essential in high-stakes machine learning tasks. However, one of the principled solutions, conformal prediction, faces challenges under limited local calibration data, privacy constraints, and data heterogeneity. In multi-agent settings, existing works do not simultaneously and satisfactorily address these challenges with guarantees either limited to averages across agents or losing validity in heterogeneous settings. Hence, we propose personalized federated weighted conformal prediction (PFWCP), a framework that combines local density ratio weighting with weighted quantile aggregation to correct for heterogeneity while preserving privacy. The method yields asymptotically valid marginal and calibration-conditional coverage guarantees for each participating agent and supports protocols with one-shot communication. Theoretical analysis presents an adjustment to the coverage variance, governed by an effective sample size expression, which is necessary in the context of weighted conformal prediction, and experiments on synthetic and real datasets show improved calibration quality over state-of-the-art federated conformal baselines.

1 Introduction

Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is a key component of modern machine learning systems, especially in high-stakes settings where decisions must be accompanied by measures of reliability (Campagner et al. 2025). Conformal prediction (CP) offers rigorous, distribution-free statistical guarantees with improved quality, in terms of tighter prediction sets and more stable coverage behavior, as the amount of quality calibration data increases (Vovk et al. 2005).

In many realistic applications, a single organization or agent may only have access to a limited amount of local data (Rieke et al. 2020). This makes it difficult to obtain both valid and efficient guarantees using CP in isolation. A possible remedy is to pool data from multiple data agents (DAs), however, in such collaborative settings, the data distributions are often heterogeneous across agents, which can lead to systematic violations of the exchangeability assumptions underpinning standard CP (Lu et al. 2023). A principled multi-agent conformal method must account for heterogeneity in how it weights and aggregates calibration information from each agent while being privacy-aware.

Existing federated conformal prediction (FCP) approaches only partially address this challenge: some methods maintain privacy and support one-shot communication but assume homogeneous data, leading to severe miscoverage under covariate shift (Humbert et al. 2023, Humbert et al. 2024), while others do not provide personalized coverage guarantees (Lu et al. 2023, Srinivasan et al. 2025, Wen et al. 2026). Some use weighted conformal prediction (WCP) to correct coverage bias but fail to correctly adjust for the shift in coverage variance, require multiple communication rounds, and typically provide only marginal coverage (MC), not calibration-conditional coverage (CCC), guarantees (Plassier et al. 2023, Plassier et al. 2024). As a result, none of them simultaneously delivers per-agent coverage guarantees, data privacy, robustness to heterogeneity, and communication efficiency.

This paper introduces a personalized federated weighted conformal prediction (PFWCP) framework that jointly corrects for bias and variance induced by data heterogeneity while preserving privacy and requiring only lightweight communication. The key idea is to combine density-ratio-based weighting of conformal scores at each agent with a weighted-quantile-of-quantiles aggregation at the server, calibrated through an approximation of the per agent CCC distribution. This yields prediction sets that (i) provide asymptotically valid MC and CCC guarantees for each participating agent under covariate shift between agents, and (ii) can be implemented in both standard and one-shot federated protocols with minimal additional overhead.

Problem formulation:

We have an interest in both MC and CCC guarantees. In the first, for a given significance level α\alpha, FCP constructs a prediction set, denoted 𝒞α\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}, which for a given test covariate XX returns a set-valued prediction with guarantee on the MC, i.e.,

ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞α​(X))≥1−α,\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X))\geq 1-\alpha,

where YY denotes the true label. Implicitly, the prediction set depends on calibration data which in the case of FCP is distributed among the participating DAs. In the second, for given significance levels α\alpha and δ\delta, FCP constructs a prediction set, denoted 𝒞α,δ\mathcal{C}_{\alpha,\delta}, providing a guarantee on the CCC, i.e.,

ℙ𝒟​(ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞α,δ​(X)|𝒟)≥1−α)≥1−δ,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\alpha,\delta}(X)|\mathcal{D})\geq 1-\alpha)\geq 1-\delta,

where we use 𝒟\mathcal{D} to denote the calibration data following distribution ℙ𝒟\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}}. The purpose of this work is to design prediction sets 𝒞α​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X) (or 𝒞α,δ​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha,\delta}(X)) in a federated setting while being efficient, i.e., minimizing the expected size of the prediction sets, while satisfying the statistical guarantees presented above.

Similarly to Min et al. (2025), we consider a federated learning (FL) scenario with KK DAs. The kk-th DA, for k∈[K]={1,…,K}k\in[K]=\{1,\dots,K\}, observes n~k\tilde{n}_{k} training data points 𝒟~k={Z~ik}i=1n~k\tilde{\mathcal{D}}^{k}=\{\tilde{Z}_{i}^{k}\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}}, Z~ik=(X~ik,Y~ik)\tilde{Z}_{i}^{k}=(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},\tilde{Y}_{i}^{k}), from unknown distribution ℙk=ℙY|X​ℙXk\mathbb{P}^{k}=\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k} on the sample space 𝒵=𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}, and nkn_{k} exchangeable calibration data points 𝒟k={Zik}i=1nk\mathcal{D}^{k}=\{Z_{i}^{k}\}_{i=1}^{n_{k}}, Zik=(Xik,Yik)Z_{i}^{k}=(X_{i}^{k},Y_{i}^{k}), from the same distribution ℙk\mathbb{P}^{k}. We denote by 𝒟=⋃k=1K𝒟k\mathcal{D}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}^{k} the total calibration data, although this data is at no point centralized. For a test point Z=(X,Y)∼ℙ=ℙY|X​ℙXZ=(X,Y)\sim\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}_{Y|X}\mathbb{P}_{X} of unknown test distribution ℙ\mathbb{P} where only XX is observed, the objective is to provide a prediction set for YY satisfying either MC or CCC guarantees.

We make the following general assumptions: (𝒜​1)(\mathcal{A}1) for each k, Z1k,…,ZnkkZ_{1}^{k},\dots,Z_{n_{k}}^{k} are exchangeable; (𝒜​2)(\mathcal{A}2) the data in 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} is independent of the data in 𝒟l\mathcal{D}^{l} for k≠lk\neq l; and (𝒜​3)(\mathcal{A}3) the data in 𝒟~=⋃k=1K𝒟~k\tilde{\mathcal{D}}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\tilde{\mathcal{D}}^{k} is independent of the data in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. We consider a practical scenario where the data is heterogeneous due to a covariate shift, i.e., ℙXk≠ℙXl\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}\neq\mathbb{P}_{X}^{l} for k≠lk\neq l, and, in line with Min et al. (2025), without loss of generality, the test data is observed by DA 11, hence, ℙ=ℙ1\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{P}^{1}. In this sense, the objective is personalization: we strive for a valid and efficient conformal predictor for each individual DA under data heterogeneity.

Preview of proposed method:

With the training data, 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}}, a prediction model is trained, in turn defining a non-conformity score function s^:𝒵→ℝ\hat{s}:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, which is evaluated on the calibration data, s^ik=s^​(Xik,Yik)\hat{s}_{i}^{k}=\hat{s}(X_{i}^{k},Y_{i}^{k}). In line with WCP, as introduced by Tibshirani et al. (2019), weight functions ω^k:𝒳→ℝ\hat{\omega}^{k}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} are defined as estimators of the density ratios ωk​(X)=[d​ℙX/d​ℙXk]​(X)\omega^{k}(X)=[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}](X) which for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} are fitted using the training data, while ω^1≡1\hat{\omega}^{1}\equiv 1, and then evaluated on the calibration data, ω^ik=ω^​(Xik)\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}=\hat{\omega}(X_{i}^{k}). We propose to use a weighted-quantile-of-quantiles method, constructing the prediction set as 𝒞β,τwqq​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ,τ}\mathcal{C}_{\beta,\tau}^{\rm wqq}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}\} for

Qβ,τ=Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δQβk),where​Qβk=Quantile⁡(1−β,∑i=1nkω^ik​δs^ik+ω^k​(X)​δ∞ω¯k+ω^k​(X)),Q_{\beta,\tau}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{Q_{\beta}^{k}}\Big),~\text{where}~~Q_{\beta}^{k}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\beta;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{k}}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)\delta_{\infty}}{\bar{\omega}^{k}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)}\Big),

where ω¯k=∑j=1nkω^jk\bar{\omega}^{k}=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{j}^{k} is the total calibration data weight, β\beta and τ\tau are the local and aggregation quantiles, respectively, and wkw_{k} are normalized weights used to emphasize contributions from DAs with higher data distribution similarity. To provide statistically valid prediction sets, quantiles β∗\beta^{*} and τ∗\tau^{*} should be determined such that 𝒞β∗,τ∗wqq​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\beta^{*},\tau^{*}}^{\rm wqq}(X) satisfies either MC or CCC guarantees. To enable this, we show in this paper that, as n1,…,nK→∞n_{1},\dots,n_{K}\to\infty,

ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β,τwqq​(X)|𝒟)→dQuantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δUβk),\mathbb{P}\big(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta,\tau}^{\rm wqq}(X)|\mathcal{D}\big)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\to}}{\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{U_{\beta}^{k}}\Big),

where Uβk∼Beta⁡((1−β)​(neffk+1),β⁡(neffk+1))U_{\beta}^{k}\sim{\rm Beta}((1-\beta)(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1),\beta(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1)) for neffk=‖[ω^1k,…,ω^nkk]‖12/‖[ω^1k,…,ω^nkk]‖22n_{\rm eff}^{k}=\|[\hat{\omega}_{1}^{k},\dots,\hat{\omega}_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{1}^{2}/\|[\hat{\omega}_{1}^{k},\dots,\hat{\omega}_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{2}^{2} which are referred to as the local effective sample sizes.

Related works:

Lu et al. (2023) introduced a notion of partial exchangeability leading to statistically valid FCP if the test distribution is a mixture of the calibration distributions and addressed privacy of score distribution via sketching. This was extended to conformal fairness by Srinivasan et al. (2025) and to group-conditional guarantees in Wen et al. (2026). Meanwhile, using the idea of WCP originally proposed by Tibshirani et al. (2019), Plassier et al. (2023) developed FCP under label shift, followed by a study for the case of covariate shift in Plassier et al. (2024) which is able to correct the coverage bias induced by the covariate shift at the cost of an increased variance. Their approach requires multiple rounds of communication for quantile estimation and provides no CCC guarantees. In another work, Li et al. (2026) study federated conformal prediction under label shift and propose a score function building on the idea of adaptive prediction sets including also a local and global prototype similarity score.

A different FCP method was proposed in Humbert et al. (2023), Humbert et al. (2024) based on the idea of sharing only a quantile of the scores and then at the central agent taking the quantile-of-quantiles, providing a privacy-preserving solution requiring just one-shot communication, contrary to FCP mentioned above. While effective for homogeneous data scenarios, severe issues arise under data heterogeneity. The proposed weighted-quantile-of-quantiles method can be viewed as a generalization of the quantile-of-quantiles approach that is designed to deal with data heterogeneity, and the quantile-of-quantiles is the particularly special case when the density ratios are constantly one, ω^k​(X)≡1\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)\equiv 1.

The idea of quantile-of-quantiles is closely related to the majority voting scheme of Cherubin (2019) which notably studies two methods: (i) the overly conservative C-method which bounds the coverage using the Markov inequality, and (ii) the overly liberal I-method that assumes independence of the events s^​(X,Y)≤Qβk\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\beta}^{k}. With this perspective, this work proposes an intermediate solution between the overly conservative C-method and overly liberal I-method.

Recently, Min et al. (2025) proposed to use decentralized data for localizing the score function employing federated engression and relying only on local data for calibration. This avoids the challenging issue with non-exchangeability in CP, however, the efficiency is restricted by the availability of local data.

A comparison of the present work with the existing literature is given in Table 1. Note that our method aim at solving all the limitations aforementioned. We are using calibration data from all agents (Fed. cali.), preserve privacy (Priv.-pres), require only one-shot communication round (One-shot) and provide MC and CCC guarantees valid for each individual agent (Pers.) under data heterogeneity (Het.) with appropriate adjustments to account for bias and variance induced by the data heterogeneity. To better see the differences between our approach and the ones proposed by Humbert et al. (2023), Humbert et al. (2024) and Min et al. (2025), we have outlined them in Figure 1.

2 Personalized federated weighted conformal prediction

We now give a detailed description of the proposed PFWCP framework. We divide the framework into three phases: (i) the training phase where the training data 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}} is used to learn the score and weight functions using federated algorithms; (ii) the calibration phase where scores and weights are evaluated on the calibration data 𝒟\mathcal{D}; and (iii) the testing phase where given a test covariate XX the conformal prediction set 𝒞α​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X) (or 𝒞α,δ​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha,\delta}(X)) is constructed.

Training phase: we begin by training a prediction model f^:𝒳→𝒴\hat{f}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} on 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}} using federated learning and define from this a non-conformity score function s^:𝒳×𝒴→ℝ\hat{s}:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}. Weight functions, defined as estimators of the density ratios [d​ℙX/d​ℙXk]​(X)[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}](X) for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\}, are trained on 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}} using federated learning and denoted ω^k\hat{\omega}^{k}, and ω^1​(X)≡1\hat{\omega}^{1}(X)\equiv 1.

Calibration phase: on the calibration data, evaluate the non-conformity scores s^ik=s^​(Xik,Yik)\hat{s}_{i}^{k}=\hat{s}(X_{i}^{k},Y_{i}^{k}) and the density ratio weights ω^ik=ω^k​(Xik)\hat{\omega}^{k}_{i}=\hat{\omega}^{k}(X_{i}^{k}) for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and i∈[nk]i\in[n_{k}], and compute local effective sample sizes neffk=‖[ω^1k,…,ω^nkk]‖12/‖[ω^1k,…,ω^nkk]‖22n_{\rm eff}^{k}=\|[\hat{\omega}_{1}^{k},\dots,\hat{\omega}_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{1}^{2}/\|[\hat{\omega}_{1}^{k},\dots,\hat{\omega}_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{2}^{2}, and normalized distribution similarity weights wkw_{k} for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\}. For a local quantile β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) and an aggregate quantile τ∈[0,1)\tau\in[0,1), the prediction set is 𝒞β,τwqq​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ,τ}\mathcal{C}_{\beta,\tau}^{\rm wqq}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}\} for

Qβ,τ=Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δQβk),where​Qβk=Quantile⁡(1−β,∑i=1nkω^ik​δs^ik+ω^k​(X)​δ∞ω¯k+ω^k​(X)).Q_{\beta,\tau}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{Q_{\beta}^{k}}\Big),~\text{where}~~Q_{\beta}^{k}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\beta;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{k}}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)\delta_{\infty}}{\bar{\omega}^{k}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)}\Big). (1)

The core principle of the proposed methodology is that the CCC for the kk-th DA can be approximated by Uβk∼Beta⁡((1−β)​(neffk+1),β⁡(neffk+1))U_{\beta}^{k}\sim{\rm Beta}((1-\beta)(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1),\beta(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1)). Specifically, according to Proposition 1, as n1,…,nK→∞n_{1},\dots,n_{K}\to\infty,

ℙ⁡(s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ,τ|𝒟)=ℙ⁡(Fs^−1​(U)≤Qβ,τ|𝒟)→dUβ(τ),\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}|\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{P}(F_{\hat{s}}^{-1}(U)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}|\mathcal{D})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\to}}U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}, (2)

where Fs^F_{\hat{s}} is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the non-conformity scores assumed to be continuous, U∼Uniform⁡([0,1])U\sim{\rm Uniform}([0,1]), and Uβ(τ)=Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δUβk)U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}={\rm Quantile}(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{U_{\beta}^{k}}).

For MC, given significance level α\alpha, we determine quantile parameters (β∗,τ∗)(\beta^{*},\tau^{*}) such that ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β∗,τ∗wqq​(X))≥1−α\mathbb{P}\big(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta^{*},\tau^{*}}^{\rm wqq}(X)\big)\geq 1-\alpha while optimizing the efficiency. This is approximately achieved by minimizing 𝔼⁡[Uβ∗(τ∗)]\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta^{*}}^{(\tau^{*})}] under constraint 𝔼⁡[Uβ∗(τ∗)]≥1−α\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta^{*}}^{(\tau^{*})}]\geq 1-\alpha, concretely

(β∗,τ∗)=arg⁡minβ,τ⁡{𝔼⁡[Uβ(τ)]:𝔼⁡[Uβ(τ)]≥1−α}.(\beta^{*},\tau^{*})=\argmin_{\beta,\tau}~~\{\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}]:\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}]\geq 1-\alpha\}. (3)

This optimization problem does not admit an analytical solution, and in fact, 𝔼⁡[Uβ(τ)]\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}] has no simple expressive formula. Rather, we approximate 𝔼⁡[Uβ(τ)]\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}] using Monte Carlo simulations, as outlined in Procedure 1. We remark here that the choice of the hyperparameter NrepN_{\rm rep} represents an important trade-off between computational complexity and the error made in solving Eq. (3). A discussion regarding setting NrepN_{\rm rep} is provided in Section S3.3.

CCC can be achieved using similar methodology as for MC. The objective is here to determine hyperparameters βc∗\beta_{c}^{*} and τc∗\tau_{c}^{*} such that the CCC is minimized while maintaining

ℙ𝒟​(ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞βc∗,τc∗wqq​(X)|𝒟)≥1−α)≥1−δ,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}}\big(\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta_{c}^{*},\tau_{c}^{*}}^{\rm wqq}(X)|\mathcal{D})\geq 1-\alpha\big)\geq 1-\delta,

for given significance levels α\alpha and δ\delta. We propose to approximate the left-side of the above inequality by ℙ⁡(Uβ(τ)≥1−α)\mathbb{P}(U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}\geq 1-\alpha) which can be numerically approximated through Monte Carlo simulations. Concretely, we replace line 7 in Procedure 1 by CCovβ,τ←1Nrep∑i=1Nrep𝟙[Uβ,i(τ)≥1−α]{\rm CCov}_{\beta,\tau}\leftarrow\frac{1}{N_{\rm rep}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{\rm rep}}\mathbbm{1}[U_{\beta,i}^{(\tau)}\geq 1-\alpha] and line 9 by (βc∗,τc∗)←arg⁡min(β,τ)∈𝒢⁡{CCovβ,τ:CCovβ,τ≥1−δ}(\beta_{c}^{*},\tau_{c}^{*})\leftarrow\argmin_{(\beta,\tau)\in\mathcal{G}}~~\{{\rm CCov}_{\beta,\tau}:{\rm CCov}_{\beta,\tau}\geq 1-\delta\}.

Testing phase: DA 1 shares the test weight ω^​(X)\hat{\omega}(X) which in turn enables the computation of the quantiles Qβ∗kQ_{\beta^{*}}^{k} (or Qβc∗kQ_{\beta^{*}_{\rm c}}^{k}). These quantiles are shared with the central server that computes the weighted-quantile-of-quantiles Qβ∗,τ∗Q_{\beta^{*},\tau^{*}} (or Qβc∗,τc∗Q_{\beta^{*}_{\rm c},\tau^{*}_{\rm c}}) and shares it with DA 1. Finally, the conformal prediction set is constructed as 𝒞β∗,τ∗wqq​(X)\mathcal{C}^{\rm wqq}_{\beta^{*},\tau^{*}}(X) (or 𝒞βc∗,τc∗wqq​(X)\mathcal{C}^{\rm wqq}_{\beta^{*}_{c},\tau^{*}_{c}}(X)).

Remark 1 (Designing the weights).

In line with the technique of Tibshirani et al. (2019), we train K−1K-1 binary classifiers, g^k:𝒳→(0,1)\hat{g}_{k}:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1), using federated learning with training data {(X~ik,0)}i=1n~k∪{(X~i1,1)}i=1n~1\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},0)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}}\cup\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{1},1)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{1}}. Then, ω^k​(X)=g^k​(X)/(1−g^k​(X))\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)=\hat{g}_{k}(X)/(1-\hat{g}_{k}(X)) where g^k​(X)\hat{g}_{k}(X) denotes the estimated probability that XX belongs to class 11 for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\}. A detailed discussion motivating this construction as well as potential alternatives is presented in Section S2.

We define aggregation weights wk∝neffkw_{k}\propto n_{\rm eff}^{k}. This choice of aggregation weights is natural as it imposes no further computation or communication overhead, and neffkn_{\rm eff}^{k} can be interpreted as a type of distribution similarity measure: a large neffkn_{\rm eff}^{k} is indicative of a high distribution similarity, and vice versa. A discussion of alternatives is given in Section S2.

One-shot personalized federated weighted conformal prediction (osPFWCP)

The PFWCP method requires each participating DA to share a quantile for each arriving test point since the quantiles in WCP changes depending on the test point covariate through the weight ω^k​(X)\hat{\omega}^{k}(X). We present now a procedure allowing the participating DAs to share only a single quantile in the calibration phase (prior to testing), and then simply adjust the outer quantile, τ\tau, depending on the arriving test covariate, in order to provide the required statistical guarantees. Thereby, the method requires only minimal communication signaling during the testing phase, however, at the cost of less flexibility in choosing the inner quantile, β\beta.

Fix an inner quantile, β˘\breve{\beta}, and construct the prediction set as 𝒞˘β˘,τwqq​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Q˘β˘,τ}\breve{\mathcal{C}}_{\breve{\beta},\tau}^{\rm wqq}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq\breve{Q}_{\breve{\beta},\tau}\} for

Q˘β˘,τ=Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δQ˘β˘k),where​Q˘β˘k=Quantile⁡(1−β˘,∑i=1nkω^ik​δs^ikω¯k).\breve{Q}_{\breve{\beta},\tau}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{\breve{Q}_{\breve{\beta}}^{k}}\Big),~\text{where}~~\breve{Q}_{\breve{\beta}}^{k}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\breve{\beta};\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{k}}}{\bar{\omega}^{k}}\Big). (4)

By doing this, the quantiles, Q˘β˘k\breve{Q}_{\breve{\beta}}^{k}, are computed and shared with the central server only once during the calibration phase, along with added information ω¯k\bar{\omega}^{k} and ω¯¯k=∑i=1nkω^ik𝟙[s^ik>Q˘β˘k]\bar{\bar{\omega}}^{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}\mathbbm{1}[\hat{s}_{i}^{k}>\breve{Q}^{k}_{\breve{\beta}}]. At the central server, given the test covariate, XX, βk\beta^{k}-quantiles such that Q˘β˘k=Qβkk\breve{Q}^{k}_{\breve{\beta}}=Q^{k}_{\beta^{k}} are derived as βk=(ω^k​(X)+ω¯¯k)/(ω¯k+ω^k​(X))\beta^{k}=(\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)+\bar{\bar{\omega}}^{k})/(\bar{\omega}^{k}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)). Finally, the central server finds a quantile τ˘∗\breve{\tau}^{*} to realize the required statistical guarantee following an algorithm similar to Procedure 1, but limiting the parameter search to the outer quantile parameter, τ\tau, and using the inner quantiles β1,…,βK\beta^{1},\dots,\beta^{K}. The complexity of this is relatively low since it is only a one-dimensional parameter search.

An overview of the communication signaling required to execute either the PFWCP or one-shot personalized federated weighted conformal prediction (osPFWCP) algorithms is given in Figure 2, illustrating clearly the benefits of the one-shot approach by noticing that minimal communication signaling is required during the testing phase.

Limitations:

The scope of the present study is limited to dealing with covariate shifts, and it will be interesting to extend the methodology to more general types of distribution shifts. Further, the presented methodology has some limitations. Namely, since the methods rely on estimating the density ratio, if this is poorly approximated, it will result in failure to properly adjust for the bias and variance in the coverage due to the data heterogeneity. Such a risk is, however, unavoidable when calibrating in the presence of unknown distribution shifts, hence, the limitation is shared with existing works (Plassier et al. 2024). Finally, some care has to be taken in the selection of the β\beta and τ\tau quantiles, mainly, it is crucial that ∑i=1nkω^ik≥(1−β)​(ω¯k+ω^k​(X))\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{i}^{k}\geq(1-\beta)(\bar{\omega}^{k}+\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)) for all k∈[K]k\in[K], otherwise QβkQ_{\beta}^{k} will not be finite. This can be dealt with by limiting the search space over β\beta and τ\tau to moderate values, see also the discussion in Section S3.3.

Key theoretical result:

The key result motivating the proposed methodology is now rigorously presented. The proof is inspired by Gretton et al. (2009) and is presented in detail in Section S1.

 

Proposition 1.

Assume that the score function is continuously distributed, that ω^k≡ωk\hat{\omega}^{k}\equiv\omega^{k}, that ℙ\mathbb{P} is absolutely continuous with respect to ℙk\mathbb{P}^{k} for k∈[K]k\in[K], and that there exists bounded constants 0<A≤1≤B0<A\leq 1\leq B such that ℙXk​(ω⁡(Xik)∈[A,B])=1\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}(\omega(X_{i}^{k})\in[A,B])=1 for Xik∼ℙXkX_{i}^{k}\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}, k∈[K]k\in[K], i∈[nk]i\in[n_{k}]. Then, as n1,…,nK→∞n_{1},\dots,n_{K}\to\infty,

ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β,τwqq​(X)|𝒟)→dQuantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δUβk),\mathbb{P}\big(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta,\tau}^{\rm wqq}(X)|\mathcal{D}\big)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\to}}{\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{U_{\beta}^{k}}\Big),

where Uβk∼Beta⁡((1−β)​(neffk+1),β⁡(neffk+1))U_{\beta}^{k}\sim{\rm Beta}((1-\beta)(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1),\beta(n_{\rm eff}^{k}+1)) for neffk=‖[ω1k,…,ωnkk]‖12/‖[ω1k,…,ωnkk]‖22n_{\rm eff}^{k}=\|[\omega_{1}^{k},\dots,\omega_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{1}^{2}/\|[\omega_{1}^{k},\dots,\omega_{n_{k}}^{k}]\|_{2}^{2}.

 

This result directly supports the core argument from Eq. (2), thereby providing the theoretical justification for Procedure 1. Notably, the approximation of Eq. (2) relies on accurate estimation of the density ratios and a sufficiently large calibration data size: as the proof indicates, the error of the approximation decays as the calibration data sizes increase. The result is complementary to that of Pournaderi and Xiang (2026) which also dealt with CCC of WCP considering the problem through concentration inequalities. Applying their result is, however, not practically straightforward in our setting due to the presence of unknown constants in the expressed CCC bounds.

We conducted a numerical experiment on the Tennessee’s student teacher achievement ratio dataset (Achilles et al. 2008), simulating data heterogeneity with exponential tilting as in Tibshirani et al. (2019) (details on the data setup are found in Section S3.4). The result is shown in Figure 3.

The quantile-of-quantiles method of Humbert et al. (2023), Humbert et al. (2024) approximates the solid blue line with the dashed red line resulting in severe miscoverage. On the other hand, Plassier et al. (2023), Plassier et al. (2024) approximates the solid purple line with the dashed red line, while we propose to approximate it with the dashed purple line. Figure 3 clearly illustrates the benefits of the proposed approximation as compared to the alternatives from the literature.

3 Numerical experiments

In this section, we report results from numerical experiments that study the performance in terms of miscoverage and efficiency of the proposed conformal predictors with those of relevant benchmarks.

The experiments cover nine datasets: two synthetic regression datasets (Gaussian and Poisson), six real regression datasets (airfoil, bike, concrete, crime, star, and protein) also considered in Tibshirani et al. (2019), Humbert et al. (2023), Humbert et al. (2024), Min et al. (2025), and a real classification dataset (cifar10c). Details regarding the datasets and how data heterogeneity is generated are found in Section S3.1. The prediction model is defined as a fully connected neural network, and likewise for the density ratio estimators. The predictors and density ratio estimators are trained in a federated learning setting and each of the K=11K=11 DAs has n~k=50\tilde{n}_{k}=50 training data points. For calibration, each DA has nk=100n_{k}=100 additional data points. Details of model specifications and training are found in Section S3.3. For the regression tasks, we use as non-conformity score s^​(X,Y)=|Y−f^​(X)|\hat{s}(X,Y)=|Y-\hat{f}(X)| where f^\hat{f} is the trained regression model, while for the classification task, we use s^​(X,Y)=1−[f^​(X)]Y\hat{s}(X,Y)=1-[\hat{f}(X)]_{Y} where [f^​(X)]Y[\hat{f}(X)]_{Y} denotes the softmax output of the trained classifier f^\hat{f} associated with the label YY.

As benchmarks we include vanilla CP (CP), federated generalized localization conformal prediction as in Min et al. (2025) (FGLCP), quantile-of-quantiles as in Humbert et al. (2023), Humbert et al. (2024) (FCP-QQ), and federated WCP Plassier et al. (2024) (FWCP). Variants of our proposal are included, herein, federated WCP by quantile-of-quantiles (FWCP-QQ), personalized federated WCP (PFWCP), one-shot personalized federated WCP (osPFWCP), and one-shot personalized federated WCP with federated generalized localization (osPFWGLCP). Details of benchmarks are given in Section S3.2.

As performance metrics, for a conformal predictor denoted 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we use the MC and CCC when relevant, and further express the conditional miscoverage (CMC), defined as 𝔼⁡[|ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞|𝒟)−(1−α)|]\mathbb{E}\big[\big|\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}|\mathcal{D})-(1-\alpha)\big|\big], and the efficiency (Eff.), defined as 𝔼⁡[|𝒞|]\mathbb{E}[|\mathcal{C}|]. These quantities are estimated through Monte Carlo simulations covering 500500 calibration data simulations with 500500 test data points for each.

Marginal coverage:

We display in Figure 4, boxplots of the coverage and efficiency with all the benchmark methodologies providing MC guarantees, on the star dataset, when setting the significance level to α=0.1\alpha=0.1. This result shows the high variability in coverage and prediction set size of CP and FGLCP due to only using local data for calibration, and also highlights the miscoverage with the FCP-QQ and FWCP-QQ methods due to failure to correct for the bias and variance shifts in the coverage caused by the data heterogeneity. Meanwhile, the proposed methods has only slight miscoverage, with low variability in coverage and prediction set size, and is generally efficient relative to the benchmarks. The most competitive benchmark for providing MC guarantees is the FWCP.

Results across all the datasets are summarized in Table 2. We observe from the results that the proposed method PFWCP satisfied the posed constraint of MC above 0.90.9 for all the datasets, while also yielding a generally low CMC, in fact the smallest in five out of the nine datasets, and being also generally efficient, in fact the most efficient in five out of the nine datasets. The proposed one-shot methods both with and without the localized scores also perform well on some of the datasets, although the decreased flexibility of the method results in a loss of valid coverage in a few cases. Integrating the localization of the scores into the proposed framework has potential to improve the efficiency as highlighted from the results on the synthetic datasets as well as the protein dataset. None of the benchmarks are capable of reaching the low miscoverage and high efficiency of the proposed methods, and it is clearly seen that the low calibration data size in the cases of CP and FGLCP, due to only using local calibration data, has severe negative implications on this. Finally, the FCP-QQ method often fails to provide the desired coverage level, which is due to the data heterogeneity. Additional complementary results with either lessened data heterogeneity is reported in Section S4, where we have also included additional benchmarks that were omitted here for conciseness.

Calibration-conditional coverage:

Results with all the benchmarks providing CCC guarantees across the datasets are summarized in Table 3, when setting the significance levels to α=0.1\alpha=0.1 and δ=0.1\delta=0.1. We observe that the proposed method PFWCP on most of the datasets, exceptions are the crime and cifar10c, the specified CCC constraint is realized, and that the gap in CCC on the crime and cifar10c datasets is relatively small compared to gap of the other FCP benchmarks. At the same time, the proposed method PFWCP achieves a much lower conditional miscoverage and a much higher efficiency than the FGLCP benchmark, as this is limited to calibrating only with local data. The osPFWCP method has severe gaps in CCC showcasing the limitations due to the lessened parameter flexibility, and a similar same observation is made for the FWCP benchmark. On the other hand, the osPFWGLCP method performs relatively well with just minor gaps in CCC while maintaining small conditional miscoverage and a high efficiency.

4 Conclusion

Personalized federated weighted conformal prediction closes an important gap between privacy-preserving collaboration of heterogeneous agents and reliable uncertainty quantification. By accounting for covariate shifts in both coverage bias and variance adjustments, it produces efficient prediction sets with more stable coverage compared to existing federated conformal methods. The presented framework motivates further studies to improve robustness of federated conformal prediction.

Proof of Proposition 1.

To that end, consider the following

ℙ⁡(s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ,τ|𝒟)=ℙ⁡(Fs^−1​(U)≤Qβ,τ|𝒟)=Fs^​(Qβ,τ),\mathbb{P}(\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}|\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{P}(F_{\hat{s}}^{-1}(U)\leq Q_{\beta,\tau}|\mathcal{D})=F_{\hat{s}}(Q_{\beta,\tau}),

where U∼Uniform⁡([0,1])U\sim{\rm Uniform}([0,1]), Fs^F_{\hat{s}} is the CDF of the scores and the second equality relies on the assumption of Fs^F_{\hat{s}} being continuous. Using that Fs^−1F_{\hat{s}}^{-1} is nondecreasing, this implies that (Humbert et al. 2024)

Qβ,τ\displaystyle Q_{\beta,\tau} =Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δQβk)→dQuantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δFs^−1​(Uβk))\displaystyle={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{Q_{\beta}^{k}}\Big)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\to}}{\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{F_{\hat{s}}^{-1}(U_{\beta}^{k})}\Big)
=Fs^−1​(Quantile⁡(1−τ,∑k=1Kwk​δUβk)),\displaystyle=F_{\hat{s}}^{-1}\Big({\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\tau;\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_{k}\delta_{U_{\beta}^{k}}\Big)\Big),

concluding the proof.

∎

We will now introduce some lemmas which will be required in the proof of Lemma 6. First, we state a known, elementary upper bound on Jensen’s gap.

 

Lemma 1.

Suppose that h:ℝ→ℝh:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} is a twice differentiable convex function for which h′′<Λh^{\prime\prime}<\Lambda for some constant Λ∈ℝ\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}, and let XX be a real-valued random variable. Then, Jensen’s gap is upper bounded by

𝔼⁡[h⁡(X)]−h⁡(𝔼⁡[X])≤12​Λ​Var​[X].\mathbb{E}[h(X)]-h(\mathbb{E}[X])\leq\frac{1}{2}\Lambda{\rm Var}[X].

 

Next we introduce Lemma 2 and Lemma 3 which are used in Lemma 6 to show that Jensen’s gap, in this case, vanishes asymptotically.

 

Lemma 2.

Let Xj∼i​i​dℙXkX_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k} for j∈[n]j\in[n] and some k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\}, X∼ℙXX\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}, and ω⁡(X)=[d​ℙX/d​ℙXk]​(X)\omega(X)=[d\mathbb{P}_{X}/d\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}](X). Assume that there exists a bounded constant B>0B>0 such that ℙX​(ω⁡(X)≤B)=1\mathbb{P}_{X}(\omega(X)\leq B)=1 and ℙXk​(ω⁡(Xj)≤B)=1\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}(\omega(X_{j})\leq B)=1 for j∈[n]j\in[n]. Proof.

By identical distribution of XjX_{j},

Var⁡[∑j=1nω⁡(Xj)+ω⁡(X)]=n⁡(𝔼⁡[ω2​(X1)]−𝔼​[ω⁡(X1)]2)+𝔼⁡[ω2​(X)]−𝔼​[ω⁡(X)]2.{\rm Var}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{n}\omega(X_{j})+\omega(X)\Big]=n\big(\mathbb{E}[\omega^{2}(X_{1})]-\mathbb{E}[\omega(X_{1})]^{2}\big)+\mathbb{E}[\omega^{2}(X)]-\mathbb{E}[\omega(X)]^{2}.

=n2(3​𝔼​[ω~te]+(n−2))2.\displaystyle=\frac{n^{2}}{\big(3\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\omega}^{\rm te}]+(n-2)\big)^{2}}.

By the almost surely boundedness of the weight function, 𝔼⁡[ω~te]\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\omega}^{\rm te}] is bounded and hence n2/(3​𝔼​[ω~te]+(n−2))2→1n^{2}/(3\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\omega}^{\rm te}]+(n-2))^{2}\to 1 as n→∞n\to\infty. Jensen’s gap can be bounded by second order properties

|𝔼⁡[n2N2​(X~te,X˘te,X3,…,Xn,X)]−n2(3​𝔼​[ω~te]+(n−2))2|≤|n22​Λn′​Var​[N⁡(X~te,X˘te,X3,…,Xn,X)]|,\begin{split}&\bigg|\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{n^{2}}{N^{2}(\tilde{X}^{\rm te},\breve{X}^{\rm te},X_{3},\dots,X_{n},X)}\Big]-\frac{n^{2}}{\big(3\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\omega}^{\rm te}]+(n-2)\big)^{2}}\bigg|\\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\leq\bigg|\frac{n^{2}}{2}\Lambda_{n}^{\prime}{\rm Var}\big[N(\tilde{X}^{\rm te},\breve{X}^{\rm te},X_{3},\dots,X_{n},X)\big]\bigg|,\end{split}

where Λn′>0\Lambda_{n}^{\prime}>0 is the smallest constant such that for a given nn, then ℙ⁡(6N4​(X~te,X˘te,X3tr,…,Xntr,X)<Λn)=1\mathbb{P}\big(\frac{6}{N^{4}(\tilde{X}^{\rm te},\breve{X}^{\rm te},X_{3}^{\rm tr},\dots,X_{n}^{\rm tr},X)}<\Lambda_{n}\big)=1. By regularity of the weight function and using Lemma 3, Λn=O⁡(1/n4)\Lambda_{n}=O(1/n^{4}), and additionally, using Lemma 2, Var⁡[N⁡(X~te,X˘te,X3,…,Xn,X)]=O⁡(n){\rm Var}\big[N(\tilde{X}^{\rm te},\breve{X}^{\rm te},X_{3},\dots,X_{n},X)\big]=O(n). Hence, Jensen’s gap is upper bounded by a term that converges to zero as n→∞n\to\infty. This implies that 𝔼⁡[n2/N2​(X~te,X˘te,X3,…,Xn,X)]→1\mathbb{E}\big[n^{2}/N^{2}(\tilde{X}^{\rm te},\breve{X}^{\rm te},X_{3},\dots,X_{n},X)\big]\to 1 as n→∞n\to\infty.

The remaining terms in Eq. (5) are quickly observed to be of order 𝔼⁡[1/N]\mathbb{E}[1/N], 𝔼⁡[1/M]\mathbb{E}[1/M], 𝔼⁡[1/N2]\mathbb{E}[1/N^{2}] or 𝔼⁡[1/M2]\mathbb{E}[1/M^{2}], and by almost surely boundedness of the weights, each of these terms are either of order 1/n1/n or 1/n21/n^{2}.

Combining the bound on the expected value and the tail bound implies the result. ∎

Appendix S2 Designing the weights

The methodology presented in Section 2 relies on two levels of weights: the local weights ω^k\hat{\omega}^{k} meant to approximate the density ratio d​ℙX/d​ℙXk{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}, and the aggregation weights wkw_{k} meant to measure distribution similarity.

Density ratio weights:

Density ratios play a central role in the context of distribution shifts in machine learning (Huang et al. 2006, Sugiyama et al. 2007, Sugiyama et al. 2008, Gretton et al. 2009, Tibshirani et al. 2019), and estimation of density ratios is in itself a large and active research field (Nguyen et al. 2007, Sugiyama et al. 2012, Choi et al. 2022, Yu et al. 2025).

In this paper, we use the method also applied by Tibshirani et al. (2019). The idea is that

ℙ⁡(X∼ℙX|X=x)ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)=ℙ⁡(X∼ℙX)ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk)​d​ℙXd​ℙXk​(x),\frac{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}|X=x)}{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x)}=\frac{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X})}{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k})}\frac{{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}}{{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}}(x),

hence, the weight ℙ⁡(X∼ℙX|X=x)/ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}|X=x)/\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x) is proportional to the density ratio [d​ℙX/d​ℙXk]​(x)[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}](x). A model trained to solve the binary classification problem of determining if an input covariate XX is sampled from ℙX\mathbb{P}_{X} or ℙXk\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}, with soft output scores g^k:𝒳→(0,1)\hat{g}^{k}:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1), exactly provides an estimate of ℙ⁡(X∼ℙX|X=x)\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}|X=x). Such a model can be fitted to the training data {(X~ik,0)}i=1n~k∪{(X~i1,1)}i=1n~1\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},0)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}}\cup\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{1},1)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{1}}. Hence, we may estimate the density ratio weights (up to proportionality) by ω^k​(X)=g^k​(X)/(1−g^k​(X))\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)=\hat{g}^{k}(X)/(1-\hat{g}^{k}(X)). Employing this approach allows for a highly flexible solution: depending on the data, the practitioner may select a suitable model for the binary classification problem. In this work, we limited our attention to fully connected neural networks, since this provides a powerful approximator well-suited for a wide variety of datasets.

If each of the KK participating DAs require calibration, the method described above in fact requires K⁡(K−1)/2K(K-1)/2 distinct binary classifiers, one for each of the pair-wise density ratios, [d​ℙXk/d​ℙXk′]​(x)[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k^{\prime}}](x) for k,k′∈[K]k,k^{\prime}\in[K], k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime}. There is another possible solution which only requires a total of KK binary classifiers. The idea is that

ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk′|X=x)=ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)ℙ⁡(X∼∑j=1KℙXj|X=x)​ℙ⁡(X∼∑j=1KℙXj|X=x)ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk′|X=x).\frac{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x)}{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k^{\prime}}|X=x)}=\frac{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x)}{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{j}|X=x)}\frac{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{j}|X=x)}{\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k^{\prime}}|X=x)}.

The density ratio ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)/ℙ⁡(X∼∑j=1KℙXj|X=x)\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x)/\mathbb{P}(X\sim\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{j}|X=x) can be estimated by training a binary classifier on ({(X~ik,1)}i=1ℓ∪{(X~ik,0)}i=ℓ+1n~k)∪(⋃k′≠k{(X~ik′,0)}i=1n~k′)\big(\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},1)\}_{i=1}^{\ell}\cup\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},0)\}_{i=\ell+1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}}\big)\cup\big(\bigcup_{k^{\prime}\neq k}\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k^{\prime}},0)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k^{\prime}}}\big) with appropriate training data weighting, for ℓ∈[n~k]\ell\in[\tilde{n}_{k}], yielding soft output scores ϱ^k:𝒳→(0,1)\hat{\varrho}^{k}:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1), thereby designing the density ratio weights (up to proportionality) by

ω^k​(X)=ϱ^1​(X)​(1−ϱ^k​(X))ϱ^k​(X)​(1−ϱ^1​(X)).\hat{\omega}^{k}(X)=\frac{\hat{\varrho}^{1}(X)(1-\hat{\varrho}^{k}(X))}{\hat{\varrho}^{k}(X)(1-\hat{\varrho}^{1}(X))}.

Another potential solution is multi-class classification. In such a setting, a model is trained on data, ⋃k=1K{(X~ik,ek)}i=1n~k\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},e_{k})\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}} where eke_{k} is the vector with 00 elements except an entry of 11 in the kk-th entry, yielding soft output scores ρ^:𝒳→(0,1)K\hat{\rho}:\mathcal{X}\to(0,1)^{K} with ∑k=1Kρ^k=1\sum_{k=1}^{K}\hat{\rho}_{k}=1. Here, ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} is an estimate of ℙ⁡(X∼ℙXk|X=x)\mathbb{P}(X\sim\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}|X=x), and the density ratios are estimated as ω^k=ρ^1/ρ^k\hat{\omega}^{k}=\hat{\rho}_{1}/\hat{\rho}_{k} for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\}. The downside of this approach is that learning a multi-class classifier is more challenging than learning a binary classifier.

The methods described above falls into the category of probabilistic classification approaches. Other methods include moment matching (Huang et al. 2006), and minimization of distribution divergences (Nguyen et al. 2007), see also Sugiyama et al. (2012) for a detailed review.

Distribution similarity weights:

The aggregation weights, wkw_{k}, can be used to provide more weight to calibration information from DAs with a higher distribution similarity. In this paper, for simplicity and to avoid additional communication overhead, we used wk∝neffkw_{k}\propto n_{\rm eff}^{k}. However, a plethora of other options could be investigated, including distribution divergence measures such as the Kullback-Leibler divergence, distribution distance metrics such as the Wasserstein metric, relative divergence measures (Yamada et al. 2011), and outlier distribution factors (Perini et al. 2023, Vejling et al. 2026).

Consider as an example the Kullback-Leibler divergence

KL⁡(ℙX,ℙXk)=∫log⁡([d​ℙX/d​ℙXk]​(X))​d​ℙX​(X).{\rm KL}\big(\mathbb{P}_{X},\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}\big)=\int{\rm log}\big([{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}](X)\big){\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}(X).

Computing the Kullback-Leibler divergence is non-trivial in practice and also has the downside of being non-symmetric in its arguments. Further, convergence rates of estimators is slow, and a more reliable solution is relative divergence measures proposed by Yamada et al. (2011). Here, the divergence between ℙX\mathbb{P}_{X} and (1−ϵ)​ℙX+ϵ​ℙXk(1-\epsilon)\mathbb{P}_{X}+\epsilon\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k} for 0<ϵ≤10<\epsilon\leq 1 is considered, and this provably improves convergence rates (Yamada et al. 2011). Another approach is based on outlier distribution factors. Here, the distribution ℙXk\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k} is expressed as a mixture between ℙX\mathbb{P}_{X} and a proper outlier distribution ℚXk\mathbb{Q}_{X}^{k}, see Blanchard et al. (2010), specifically, ℙXk=(1−π)​ℙX+π​ℚXk\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}=(1-\pi)\mathbb{P}_{X}+\pi\mathbb{Q}_{X}^{k} for an outlier factor 0<π≤10<\pi\leq 1. The outlier factor directly provides a measure of distribution similarity and there exists practical methods for estimating it (Perini et al. 2023, Vejling et al. 2026).

Appendix S3 Additional data and implementation details

S3.1 Details regarding datasets

Synthetic Gaussian data:

This synthetic data is generated by sampling covariates Xik∼i​i​d𝒩⁡(γk,1)X_{i}^{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(\gamma_{k},1) for the kk-th data agent where γk∈ℝd\gamma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and d=10d=10 is the dimensionality. The response variable is defined as Yik=∑l=1d[Xik]lY_{i}^{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{d}[X_{i}^{k}]_{l}. We evaluate three setting with varying degrees of data heterogeneity. In the severe case, data heterogeneity is simulated by sampling [γ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([−1,−0.5])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-1,-0.5])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [γk]l∼i​i​dUniform([−0.7,0.7])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-0.7,0.7])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. In the moderate case, data heterogeneity is simulated by sampling [γ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([−0.5,−0.25])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-0.5,-0.25])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [γk]l∼i​i​dUniform([−0.35,0.35])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-0.35,0.35])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. In the mild case, data heterogeneity is simulated by sampling [γ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([−0.25,−0.125])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-0.25,-0.125])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [γk]l∼i​i​dUniform([−0.175,0.175])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\gamma_{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([-0.175,0.175])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. The density ratios [d​ℙ/d​ℙk]​(X)[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}^{k}](X) are known as ratios of Gaussian densities, which allows for the use of oracle weights in the numerical experiments. The severe case is the one studied in Section 3.

Synthetic Poisson data:

This synthetic data is generated by sampling covariates Xik∼i​i​d𝒩⁡(3+γk,1)X_{i}^{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(3+\gamma_{k},1) for the kk-th data agent where γk∈ℝd\gamma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and d=10d=10 is the dimensionality. In line with (Humbert et al. 2023), the response variable is defined as

Yik|Xik∼i​i​dPoisson(sin2(X¯ik)+0.1)+0.03X¯ik𝒩(0,1)+𝟙[Uniform([0,1])<0.01]𝒩(0,5),Y_{i}^{k}|X_{i}^{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Poisson}({\rm sin}^{2}(\bar{X}_{i}^{k})+0.1)+0.03\bar{X}_{i}^{k}\mathcal{N}(0,1)+\mathbbm{1}[{\rm Uniform}([0,1])<0.01]\mathcal{N}(0,5),

where X¯ik=∑l=1d[Xik]l\bar{X}_{i}^{k}=\sum_{l=1}^{d}[X_{i}^{k}]_{l}. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the synthetic Gaussian data.

Airfoil data (Brooks et al. 1989):

This NASA dataset arose from studying different sizes of NACA 00120012 airfoils under various conditions. It consists of 15031503 instances of d=5d=5 covariates and 11 response. The covariates are frequency in Hertz, angle of attack in degrees, chord length in meters, free-stream velocity in meters per second, and suction side displacement thickness in meters. The covariates are normalized using the min-max rule. The response is the scaled sound pressure level in decibels. The frequency and suction side displacement thickness are log-transformed in our numerical experiments.

Data heterogeneity is simulated using exponential tilting as in Tibshirani et al. (2019). This is done as it allows the oracle baseline to know the true density ratio weights up to proportionality. For each data agent k∈[K]k\in[K], data points are sampled with replacement with probabilities proportional to exp⁡(X⊤​ζk){\rm exp}(X^{\top}\zeta^{k}) where ζk∈ℝd\zeta^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are tilting arrays. By construction, [d​ℙ/d​ℙk]​(X)∝exp⁡(X⊤​(ζ1−ζk))[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}/{\rm d}\mathbb{P}^{k}](X)\propto{\rm exp}(X^{\top}(\zeta^{1}-\zeta^{k})). We evaluate three setting with varying degrees of data heterogeneity. In the severe case, we generate [ζ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([1,3])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([1,3])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [ζk]l∼i​i​dUniform([0,2])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,2])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. In the moderate case, we generate [ζ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([0.5,1.5])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0.5,1.5])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [ζk]l∼i​i​dUniform([0,1])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,1])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. In the mild case, we generate [ζ1]l∼i​i​dUniform([0.25,0.75])𝟙[l≤⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{1}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0.25,0.75])\mathbbm{1}[l\leq\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for l∈[d]l\in[d] and [ζk]l∼i​i​dUniform([0,0.5])𝟙[l>⌊d/4⌋][\zeta^{k}]_{l}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,0.5])\mathbbm{1}[l>\lfloor d/4\rfloor] for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} and l∈[d]l\in[d]. The severe case is the one studied in Section 3.

Bike data (Fanaee-T and Gama 2013):

With this dataset we are predicting hourly bike sharing renting counts in Washington, D.C., and the data contains 1737917379 instances with d=9d=9 covariates and 11 response. The covariates are the hour of the day, whether it is a holiday (if it is a holiday it is 1, otherwise it is 0), the day of the week, whether it is a working day (if day is neither weekend nor holiday it is 1, otherwise it is 0), the weather (1 means clear sky or few clouds, 2 means cloudy, 3 means light precipitation, 4 means heavy precipitation), normalized temperature (Celsius divided by 41), normalized feeling temperature (Celsius divided by 50), relative humidity, and normalized wind speed (meters per second divided by 67). The covariates are normalized using the min-max rule. The response is the hourly bike sharing renting counts. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the airfoil data.

Concrete data (Yeh 1998):

This concrete compressive strength dataset consists of 10301030 instances with d=8d=8 covariates and 11 response. The covariates are concentrations in kilograms per cubic meter of cement, blast furnace slag, fly ash, water, superplasticizer, coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, and age given in days. The covariates are normalized using the min-max rule. The response is the concrete compressive strength measured in megapascals. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the airfoil data.

Crime data (Redmond 2009):

This dataset concerns the prediction of violent crimes across communities in the US containing 19941994 instances with d=41d=41 covariates and 11 response. The covariates cover aspects of demographic composition, socioeconomic status, labor market, and law enforcement presence. The covariates are normalized using the min-max rule. The response is the total number of violent crimes per 10510^{5} population. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the airfoil data.

Star data (Achilles et al. 2008):

This arose from studying how pupil-teacher ratios impact student performance in Tennessee. The dataset contains 37543754 instances with d=20d=20 covariates and 11 response. The covariates cover aspects of student background and demographics, teacher characteristics, classroom and treatment assignment, and school-level attributes. The covariates are normalized using the min-max rule. The response is the achievement score. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the airfoil data.

Protein data (Rana 2013):

This dataset deals with physicochemical properties of protein tertiary structure and consists of 4573045730 instances with d=9d=9 covariates and 11 response. The covariates are the total surface area, the non-polar exposed area, the fractional area of exposed non-polar residue, the fractional area of exposed non-polar part of the residue, the molecular mass weighted exposed area, the average deviation from the standard exposed area of residue, the Euclidean distance, the secondary structure penalty, and the spatial distribution constraints. The response is the size of the residue. Data heterogeneity is simulated in the same way as for the airfoil data.

CIFAR-10 data (Hendrycks and Dietterich 2019):

The CIFAR-10 data is a well-studied image classification dataset of 6000060000 total instances with labels airplane, automobile, bird, cat, deer, dog, frog, horse, ship, and truck with images in resolution d=32×32×3d=32\times 32\times 3. The CIFAR-10C dataset consists of the CIFAR-10 data contaminated with various types of noise of varying levels of severity (from 0-4). We restrict our attention to the brightness contamination, and evaluate three setting with varying degrees of data heterogeneity. In the severe case, we simulate data heterogeneity by sampling images random uniformly and contaminating the images with severity level s∈{0,1,2,3,4}s\in\{0,1,2,3,4\} with probability proportional to [ηk]s∼i​i​dUniform⁡([0,1])[\eta^{k}]_{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,1]) for k∈[K]k\in[K]. In the moderate case, we simulate data heterogeneity by sampling images random uniformly and contaminating the images with severity level s∈{0,1,2}s\in\{0,1,2\} with probability proportional to [ηk]s∼i​i​dUniform⁡([0,1])[\eta^{k}]_{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,1]) for k∈[K]k\in[K]. In the mild case, we simulate data heterogeneity by sampling images random uniformly and contaminating the images with severity level s∈{0,1}s\in\{0,1\} with probability proportional to [ηk]s∼i​i​dUniform⁡([0,1])[\eta^{k}]_{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle iid}}{{\sim}}{\rm Uniform}([0,1]) for k∈[K]k\in[K]. The severe case is the one studied in Section 3.

S3.2 Details of benchmarks

CP:

Standard CP calibrates using local scores s^11,…,s^n11\hat{s}_{1}^{1},\dots,\hat{s}_{n_{1}}^{1}. To achieve MC at level α\alpha, the local quantile Qα=Quantile⁡(1−α,1n1+1​(∑i=1n1δs^i1+δ∞))Q_{\alpha}={\rm Quantile}\big(1-\alpha;\frac{1}{n_{1}+1}\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n_{1}}\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{1}}+\delta_{\infty}\big)\big) is computed and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qα}\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\alpha}\}. To achieve CCC given levels α\alpha and δ\delta, α∗\alpha^{*} is determined as the largest α′\alpha^{\prime} such that FBeta​(1−α,(1−α′)​(n1+1),α′​(n1+1))≤δF_{\rm Beta}(1-\alpha;(1-\alpha^{\prime})(n_{1}+1),\alpha^{\prime}(n_{1}+1))\leq\delta where FBetaF_{\rm Beta} is the CDF of the Beta distribution. The local quantile Qα∗Q_{\alpha^{*}} is then evaluated, and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α∗​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha^{*}}(X).

FGLCP (Min et al. 2025):

This baseline corresponds to PFCP2 of Min et al. (2025). First, the dataset 𝒟1\mathcal{D}^{1} is split into two disjoint datasets 𝒟eng1\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm eng} and 𝒟cal1\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm cal}, where 𝒟eng1\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm eng} will be used for the engression task and 𝒟cal1\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm cal} is used for the model calibration. The method then uses datasets 𝒟eng1\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm eng} and 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} for k∈{2,…,K}k\in\{2,\dots,K\} to approximate the conditional distribution F​(s^​(X,Y)|X)F(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X), yielding localized scores s^loc​(X,Y)=F^​(s^​(X,Y)|X)\hat{s}_{\rm loc}(X,Y)=\hat{F}(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X) for (X,Y)∈𝒟cal1(X,Y)\in\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm cal}. The conformal prediction set is then constructed as 𝒞αglcp={Y∈𝒴:s^loc​(X,Y)≤Qαglcp}\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}^{\rm glcp}=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}_{\rm loc}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\alpha}^{\rm glcp}\} where

Qαglcp=Quantile⁡(1−α,1|𝒟cal1|+1​(∑(X,Y)∈𝒟cal1δs^loc​(X,Y)+δ1)).Q_{\alpha}^{\rm glcp}={\rm Quantile}\Big(1-\alpha;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm cal}|+1}\Big(\sum_{(X,Y)\in\mathcal{D}^{1}_{\rm cal}}\delta_{\hat{s}_{\rm loc}(X,Y)}+\delta_{1}\Big)\Big).

To compute F^​(s^​(X,Y)|X)\hat{F}(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X), a federated engression algorithm is employed based on a fully connected neural network with two hidden layers each with 50 hidden units followed by Platt calibration. The engression data is randomly split in a 9:1 ratio for classifier training and Platt calibration. The reader is referred Min et al. (2025) for further details on the federated engression algorithm used to compute F^​(s^​(X,Y)|X)\hat{F}(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X).

FCP:

Standard FCP aggregates all the scores s^ik\hat{s}_{i}^{k} for k∈[K]k\in[K] and i∈[nk]i\in[n_{k}]. To achieve MC at level α\alpha, the quantile Qα=Quantile⁡(1−α:1∑k=1Knk+1​(∑k=1K∑i=1nkδs^ik+δ∞))Q_{\alpha}={\rm Quantile}\big(1-\alpha:\frac{1}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}+1}\big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{k}}+\delta_{\infty}\big)\big) is computed and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qα}\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\alpha}\}. To achieve CCC given levels α\alpha and δ\delta, α∗\alpha^{*} is determined as the largest α′\alpha^{\prime} such that

FBeta​(1−α,(1−α′)​(∑k=1Knk+1),α′​(∑k=1Knk+1))≤δ,F_{\rm Beta}\Big(1-\alpha;(1-\alpha^{\prime})\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}+1\Big),\alpha^{\prime}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}+1\Big)\Big)\leq\delta,

where FBetaF_{\rm Beta} is the CDF of the Beta distribution. The local quantile Qα∗Q_{\alpha^{*}} is then evaluated, and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α∗​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha^{*}}(X).

FCP-QQ (Humbert et al. 2023, Humbert et al. 2024):

For MC guarantee at level α\alpha, the quantile-of-quantiles method finds quantiles β¯\bar{\beta} and τ¯\bar{\tau} by solving

(β¯,τ¯)=arg⁡min(β,τ)∈(0,1)2⁡{𝔼⁡[Uβ(⌈K⁡(1−τ)⌉)]:𝔼⁡[Uβ(⌈K⁡(1−τ)⌉)]≥1−α},(\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau})=\argmin_{(\beta,\tau)\in(0,1)^{2}}~~\{\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\lceil K(1-\tau)\rceil)}]:\mathbb{E}[U_{\beta}^{(\lceil K(1-\tau)\rceil)}]\geq 1-\alpha\},

where Uβk∼Beta⁡((1−β)​(nk+1),β⁡(nk+1))U_{\beta}^{k}\sim{\rm Beta}((1-\beta)(n_{k}+1),\beta(n_{k}+1)), and Uβ(t)U_{\beta}^{(t)} is the tt-th smallest among Uβ1,…,UβKU_{\beta}^{1},\dots,U_{\beta}^{K}. This is solvable using that Uβ(⌈K⁡(1−τ)⌉)U_{\beta}^{(\lceil K(1-\tau)\rceil)} follows a Beta-Beta distribution. Given the quantiles β¯\bar{\beta} and τ¯\bar{\tau}, the quantile-of-quantiles Qβ¯,τ¯=Quantile⁡(1−τ¯,1K​∑k=1KδQβ¯k)Q_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}={\rm Quantile}\big(1-\bar{\tau};\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{Q_{\bar{\beta}}^{k}}\big) where Qβ¯k=Quantile⁡(1−β¯,1nk+1​(∑j=1nkδs^jk+δ∞))Q_{\bar{\beta}}^{k}={\rm Quantile}\big(1-\bar{\beta};\frac{1}{n_{k}+1}\big(\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}\delta_{\hat{s}_{j}^{k}}+\delta_{\infty}\big)\big) is computed and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞β¯,τ¯​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ¯,τ¯}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}\}. Likewise, the CCC guarantee with levels α\alpha and δ\delta can be satisfied by finding quantiles β¯c\bar{\beta}_{\rm c} and τ¯c\bar{\tau}_{\rm c} minimizing the CCC while maintaining

ℙ𝒟​(ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞βc,τc​(X)|𝒟)≥1−α)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{D}}\big(\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}_{\beta_{c},\tau_{c}}(X)|\mathcal{D})\geq 1-\alpha\big)\geq 1-\delta.

This can practically be realized by exploiting that the left-hand side of the above inequality is equal to ℙ⁡(Uβc(⌈K⁡(1−τc)⌉)≥1−α)\mathbb{P}\big(U_{\beta_{c}}^{(\lceil K(1-\tau_{c})\rceil)}\geq 1-\alpha\big) and again using that Uβc(⌈K⁡(1−τc)⌉)U_{\beta_{c}}^{(\lceil K(1-\tau_{c})\rceil)} follows a Beta-Beta distribution.

FWCP (Plassier et al. 2023, Plassier et al. 2024):

The federated weighted conformal prediction (FWCP) approach uses all the scores s^ik\hat{s}_{i}^{k} for k∈[K]k\in[K] and i∈[nk]i\in[n_{k}] to determine the quantile of the score distribution weighted by an estimate, ω^′\hat{\omega}^{\prime}, of ω′​(X)=[d​ℙX/∑k=2Kd​ℙXk/(K−1)]​(X)\omega^{\prime}(X)=[{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}/\sum_{k=2}^{K}{\rm d}\mathbb{P}_{X}^{k}/(K-1)](X). The density ratio is estimated by fitting a binary classifier to data {(X~i1,1)}i=1n~1∪(⋃k=2K{(X~ik,0)}i=1n~k)\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{1},1)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{1}}\cup\big(\bigcup_{k=2}^{K}\{(\tilde{X}_{i}^{k},0)\}_{i=1}^{\tilde{n}_{k}}\big). As the binary classifier we employ a fully connected neural network with a single hidden layer using the standard implementation in scikit-learn. To achieve MC at level α\alpha, the quantile

Qα=Quantile⁡(1−α:∑k=1K∑i=1nkω^′​(Xik)​δs^ik+ω^′​(X)​δ∞∑k=1K∑i=1nkω^′​(Xik)+ω^′​(X)),Q_{\alpha}={\rm Quantile}\bigg(1-\alpha:\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X_{i}^{k})\delta_{\hat{s}_{i}^{k}}+\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X)\delta_{\infty}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X_{i}^{k})+\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X)}\bigg),

is computed and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qα}\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\alpha}\}. To achieve CCC given levels α\alpha and δ\delta, α∗\alpha^{*} is determined as the largest α′\alpha^{\prime} such that

FBeta​(1−α,(1−α′)​(∑k=1Knk+1),α′​(∑k=1Knk+1))≤δ,F_{\rm Beta}\Big(1-\alpha;(1-\alpha^{\prime})\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}+1\Big),\alpha^{\prime}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}n_{k}+1\Big)\Big)\leq\delta,

where FBetaF_{\rm Beta} is the CDF of the Beta distribution. The local quantile Qα∗Q_{\alpha^{*}} is then evaluated, and the prediction set is constructed as 𝒞α∗​(X)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha^{*}}(X).

FWCP-QQ (ours):

A variant of FWCP using a quantile-of-quantiles approach is also included as a benchmark. The quantiles β¯\bar{\beta} and τ¯\bar{\tau} satisfying the MC condition are found as in the FCP-QQ approach. Given the quantiles β¯\bar{\beta} and τ¯\bar{\tau}, compute Qβ¯,τ¯=Quantile⁡(1−τ¯:1K​∑k=1KδQβ¯k)Q_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}={\rm Quantile}\big(1-\bar{\tau}:\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{Q_{\bar{\beta}}^{k}}\big) where Qβ¯kQ_{\bar{\beta}}^{k} is the weighted quantile

Qβ¯k=Quantile⁡(1−β¯:∑j=1nkω^j′​δs^jk+ω^′​(X)​δ∞ω¯′+ω^′​(X)),Q_{\bar{\beta}}^{k}={\rm Quantile}\bigg(1-\bar{\beta}:\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n_{k}}\hat{\omega}_{j}^{\prime}\delta_{\hat{s}_{j}^{k}}+\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X)\delta_{\infty}}{\bar{\omega}^{\prime}+\hat{\omega}^{\prime}(X)}\bigg),

using the same weights as for FWCP. The prediction set is constructed as 𝒞β¯,τ¯​(X)={Y∈𝒴:s^​(X,Y)≤Qβ¯,τ¯}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}(X)=\{Y\in\mathcal{Y}:\hat{s}(X,Y)\leq Q_{\bar{\beta},\bar{\tau}}\}. Likewise, the CCC guarantee with levels α\alpha and δ\delta can be satisfied by finding quantiles β¯c\bar{\beta}_{\rm c} and τ¯c\bar{\tau}_{\rm c} as in FCP-QQ.

PFWCP (ours):

This is the core methodology presented in Section 2.

osPFWCP (ours):

This is the communication efficient one-shot method detailed in Section 2.

osPFWGLCP (ours):

This benchmark is a variant of the osPFWCP in which federated engression is used to localize the score function as in the FGLCP benchmark proposed by Min et al. (2025). Hence, this method combines the benefits of score function localization of Min et al. (2025) with the federation of calibration information with personalized statistical validity of this work. The baseline divides the datasets 𝒟k\mathcal{D}^{k} into two disjoint datasets 𝒟engk\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm eng} and 𝒟calk\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm cal} with a 1:1 ratio, where 𝒟engk\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm eng} will be used for the engression task and 𝒟calk\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm cal} is used for the model calibration. The method then uses datasets 𝒟engk\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm eng} for k∈[K]k\in[K] to approximate the conditional distribution F​(s^​(X,Y)|X)F(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X), yielding localized scores s^loc​(X,Y)=F^​(s^​(X,Y)|X)\hat{s}_{\rm loc}(X,Y)=\hat{F}(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X) for (X,Y)∈⋃k=1K𝒟calk(X,Y)\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal{D}^{k}_{\rm cal}. The conformal prediction set is then constructed using the weighted-quantile-of-quantiles approach with one-shot communication as presented in Section 2, using s^loc\hat{s}_{\rm loc} in place of s^\hat{s}. As in the FGLCP benchmark, F^​(s^​(X,Y)|X)\hat{F}(\hat{s}(X,Y)|X) is computed using a federated engression algorithm based on a fully connected neural network with two hidden layers each with 50 hidden units followed by Platt calibration. The engression data is randomly split in a 9:1 ratio for classifier training and Platt calibration.

S3.3 Additional implementation details

Prediction model specifications and training:

The prediction model is given by a fully connected neural network trained with federated learning on the training data of all the participating data agents. For the synthetic datasets, two hidden layers each with 3030 hidden units is used. For the real regression datasets, three hidden layers are used with 500500, 200200, and 100100 hidden units, respectively. For the cifar10 data, three hidden layers are used with 200200, 100100, and 5050 hidden units, respectively, acting on the principal components trained to explain at least 90%90~\% of the variance.

For the regression tasks, the hidden layer activations are LeakyReLu, and the neural networks are trained using the adam algorithm with the mean squared error loss. The batch size is 3232, the learning rate is 0.0010.001, and the number of epochs is 50005000.

For the classification task, the hidden layer activations are ReLu with softmax output activation, and the neural networks are trained using the adam algorithm with the cross entropy loss and an L2L_{2} regularization term with parameter 0.00010.0001. The batch size is 3232, the learning rate is 0.0010.001, and the number of epochs is 50005000.

Density ratio estimation:

For the synthetic datasets, the binary classifiers used to estimate the density ratios are specified as fully connected neural networks with a single 1010-unit hidden layer employing ReLu hidden layer activations with sigmoid output activation. For the real regression datasets, we use a single 3030-unit hidden layer. For the cifar10 dataset, we use also a fully connected neural network with a single 1010-unit hidden layer, here acting on the principal components trained to explain at least 90%90~\% of the variance. The neural networks are trained using the adam algorithm with the cross entropy loss and an L2L_{2} regularization term with parameter 0.00010.0001. The batch size is set to 200200, the learning rate is set to 0.0010.001, and the number of epochs used is 600600.

Hyperparameter selection:

The choice of NrepN_{\rm rep} (see Procedure 1) represents an important trade-off between computational complexity and the error made in solving Eq. (3). The algorithm simulates data Uβ,i(τ)≃ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β,τwqq​(X)|𝒟)U_{\beta,i}^{(\tau)}\simeq\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}^{\rm wqq}_{\beta,\tau}(X)|\mathcal{D}) and, for MC, uses the sample mean to approximate ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β,τwqq​(X))=𝔼⁡[ℙ⁡(Y∈𝒞β,τwqq​(X)|𝒟)]\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}^{\rm wqq}_{\beta,\tau}(X))=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{P}(Y\in\mathcal{C}^{\rm wqq}_{\beta,\tau}(X)|\mathcal{D})]. The variance of the sample mean equals Var⁡[Uβ,i(τ)]/Nrep{\rm Var}[U_{\beta,i}^{(\tau)}]/N_{\rm rep}. Since Uβ,i(τ)U_{\beta,i}^{(\tau)} are random variables defined on [0,1][0,1], their variance is upper bounded by 1/41/4, meaning that the standard deviation of the sample mean is upper bounded by 1/(2​Nrep)1/(2\sqrt{N_{\rm rep}}). Practically, it is desirable to have 1/(2​Nrep)≪α1/(2\sqrt{N_{\rm rep}})\ll\alpha, i.e., Nrep≫1/(4​α2)N_{\rm rep}\gg 1/(4\alpha^{2}). For CCC we are concerned with the variance of the empirical quantile estimator which has asymptotic expansion α⁡(1−α)/(Nrep​f2​(F−1​(1−α)))\alpha(1-\alpha)/(N_{\rm rep}f^{2}(F^{-1}(1-\alpha))) where F−1F^{-1} and ff are the quantile and density functions of Uβ(τ)U_{\beta}^{(\tau)}, respectively (Stuart and Ord 1994), leading to the guideline Nrep≫α⁡(1−α)/(δ2​f2​(F−1​(1−α)))N_{\rm rep}\gg\alpha(1-\alpha)/(\delta^{2}f^{2}(F^{-1}(1-\alpha))). Since ff and F−1F^{-1} are unknown prior to running the algorithm, this is not directly applicable but the expression is inverse proportional to δ2\delta^{2} giving some intuition still. In the numerical experiments, we use Nrep=2000N_{\rm rep}=2000 for MC guarantees, and Nrep=4000N_{\rm rep}=4000 for CCC guarantees.

In Procedure 1, a search space 𝒢⊂(0,1)×[0,1)\mathcal{G}\subset(0,1)\times[0,1) on the quantiles (β,τ)(\beta,\tau) must be provided. In this work, we design this as {α,α+Δβ​…,1/4}×{0,Δτ,…,1/2}\{\alpha,\alpha+\Delta_{\beta}\dots,1/4\}\times\{0,\Delta_{\tau},\dots,1/2\} where Δβ=(1/4−α)/21\Delta_{\beta}=(1/4-\alpha)/21 and Δτ=1/42\Delta_{\tau}=1/42 are the step sizes. This ensures that β∗\beta^{*} is never small to the point of risking Qβ∗kQ_{\beta^{*}}^{k} being infinite, and generally, a value of β\beta closer to 1/21/2 provides more stable prediction sets. For the one-shot procedures, osPFWCP and osPFWGLCP, the search space is only on the τ\tau quantile and is designed as {0,Δτ′,…,1−max⁡(w1,…,wK)}\{0,\Delta^{\prime}_{\tau},\dots,1-{\rm max}(w_{1},\dots,w_{K})\} where Δτ′=(1−max⁡(w1,…,wK))/50\Delta^{\prime}_{\tau}=(1-{\rm max}(w_{1},\dots,w_{K}))/50, thereby ensuring that 1−τ∗1-\tau^{*} is always greater than max⁡(w1,…,wK){\rm max}(w_{1},\dots,w_{K}) such that a valid quantile can be determined.

S3.4 Details to reproduce Figure 3

To illustrate the core principle motivated by Proposition 1, we conducted a numerical experiment on the Tennessee’s student teacher achievement ratio dataset (Achilles et al. 2008). With this data, we evaluated the CCC for CP with and without covariate shift, WCP with weights estimated using logistic regression, as well as CP without covariate shift using the estimated effective sample size. As in Tibshirani et al. (2019), we simulated a covariate shift through exponential tilting, specifically, the calibration data with covariate shift samples the dataset with replacement with probabilities proportional to exp⁡(X⊤​ζ){\rm exp}(X^{\top}\zeta) where ζ=−[2.5,1,2,1,0.5,1.5,1,1.5,0.5,0.5,0,0.5,0.5,0,0,0.5,1.5,2.5,2,0]⊤\zeta=-[2.5,1,2,1,0.5,1.5,1,1.5,0.5,0.5,0,0.5,0.5,0,0,0.5,1.5,2.5,2,0]^{\top}. The elements of this tilting array were generated random uniformly from {0,−0.5,−1,…,−3}\{0,-0.5,-1,\dots,-3\}. The significance level was set to α=0.1\alpha=0.1, and the calibration dataset had n=100n=100 samples. The empirical CCC is evaluated for 10001000 Monte Carlo simulations of the calibration data with 10001000 test points for each. The result is shown in Figure 3.

Appendix S4 Additional numerical results

Here, we provide additional numerical results to supplement those presented in Section 3. This includes results with additional benchmarks, specifically, FCP and the proposed methods using oracle weights (when these are known). Further, we include results with the three different levels of heterogeneity described in Section S3.1. Tables 4 and 5 shows extended versions of the Tables 2 and 3, i.e., the severe heterogeneity experiments. Tables 6 and 7 show results for the case of moderate heterogeneity while Tables 8 and 9 show the results for the case of mild heterogeneity. Overall, the results indicate the efficacy of the proposed PFWCP method to efficiently provide the specified statistical guarantees. Meanwhile, the one-shot techniques osPFWCP and osPFWGLCP show promising performance to provide MC guarantees but on occasion struggles to provide the specified CCC guarantees, due to the lessened flexibility in the quantile specifications. Using osPFWGLCP tends to provide efficient conformal prediction sets with less miscoverage than osPFWCP. Comparatively, the FWCP-QQ benchmark tends to be overly conservative, which is also to be expected considering that it does not adjust for the increased variance in the coverage due to the data heterogeneity. The FWCP benchmark is competitive in terms of providing MC guarantees, but tends to fail dramatically in satisfying CCC guarantees. A similar remark applies to the FCP and FCP-QQ benchmarks, although these techniques tend to be overly liberal in terms of both MC and CCC guarantees in the case of severe heterogeneity.
